slides.1.highlights.1.title: Self-marking
slides.1.highlights.1.content: After each short answer the marking points appear; tick honestly only the points you actually wrote; covering at least 60% passes that question

slides.1.highlights.2.content: For missed points, revisit the relevant level; rewrite the same question a few days later to measure progress

slides.2.componentProps.slide.title: 📋 Mock exam
What is downy mildew usually controlled with?
A. Irrigation
B. Copper
C. Sulphur
D. Grafting
Sulphur is for powdery mildew.
What is the minimum lees ageing for Cava Reserva?
A. 30 months
B. 36 months
C. 18 months
D. 9 months
Gran Reserva 30, Paraje Calificado 36.
What happens when Oloroso is fortified to about 17% or more?
A. It becomes sweet
B. A second fermentation starts
C. The colour gets paler
D. Flor cannot survive; purely oxidative ageing
Flor survives only at about 15%.
In markets with per-bottle duty, why is cheap wine poor value?
A. Fixed duty and packaging take a large share of the price
B. Cheap wine has more alcohol
C. Cheap wine cannot be exported
D. Cheap wine always uses natural cork
The wine itself is a small share of the value.
Short answer: explain how the timing of fortification in Port decides its sweetness and winemaking. (about 150 words)
Grape spirit at about 77% added part-way through fermentation
High alcohol stops the yeast → residual sugar → sweet style
Fermentation lasts only two or three days → extraction must be fast and intense
Methods: treading in lagares, robotic treading, autovinifiers

Port is fortified part-way through fermentation with grape spirit at about 77%; the high alcohol stops the yeast and unfermented sugar remains, so it is sweet. Because fermentation lasts only two or three days, colour and tannin must be extracted quickly: traditionally by treading in stone lagares, now with robotic treaders or autovinifiers.
Short answer: assess the different effects of warming on sparkling wine in England and in warm regions. (about 200 words)
England: more reliable ripening and less volatile yields → benefits
England’s other assets: chalk, cool climate, Champagne investment, Sussex PDO
Warm regions: harder to keep acidity → earlier picking, altitude, acidification
Risk: England still faces spring frost and vintage variation
Conclusion: a conditional verdict (benefit or harm depends on the starting climate)

Warming makes ripening in marginal regions such as England more reliable and yields less volatile; together with chalk soils, Champagne investment and the 2022 Sussex PDO, England benefits overall, though spring frost and vintage variation remain. Warm regions find it harder to keep acidity and must pick earlier, move uphill or acidify, raising cost and stylistic pressure. Conclusion: the effect depends on the starting climate, an opportunity for marginal regions and a challenge for warm ones.
